findings.issue_text: [BUG] sync_group_assignee_outbound puts AssignmentSource.to_dict() output containing a raw datetime object into Celery task kwargs, which the default JSON serializer cannot encode. AssignmentSource.to_dict() returns asdict(self), and dataclasses.asdict copies the `queued` datetime through unchanged — it is not converted to a string. When assignment_source is non-None (i.e., on every inbound-initiated assignment, the exact case the feature exists for), sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs={..."assignment_source_dict": {"queued": <datetime>...}}) raises kombu EncodeError at enqueue time, so the outbound sync never runs and the cross-integration propagation this PR implements silently fails in production while passing in tests (with self.tasks() bypasses real serialization).

[BUG] The `queued` field default `timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class-definition (import) time, so every AssignmentSource constructed without an explicit `queued` shares a single stale timestamp frozen at worker/process import. Any consumer relying on `queued` to order or dedupe sync events (the field name implies exactly that) gets the module-import time for all sources created in a process's lifetime — e.g., a long-lived region-silo worker reports hours- or days-old queue times. The bug is invisible in the added tests because they only assert `queued is not None`.

[ADVISORY] from_dict performs no type coercion for `queued`, so after any real dict round-trip through JSON (or a future fix that serializes the datetime as an ISO string), `queued` will be a str despite the declared datetime type. Downstream code that treats `assignment_source.queued` as a datetime (sorting, arithmetic, timezone-aware comparisons) raises TypeError once the payload crosses a serialization boundary — the very boundary this dataclass exists to cross via to_dict/from_dict.

[ADVISORY] The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains an `assignment_source` parameter that no call site in this diff passes and no concrete implementation uses, while its sibling `should_sync`/`sync_assignee_outbound` changes are the ones actually wired to AssignmentSource. Concrete implementations across providers (Jira, GitHub, VSTS, etc.) whose signatures lack **kwargs would raise TypeError the first time a caller does pass `assignment_source=`; in this diff the parameter is dead surface area that a future caller can pass without any tested consumer — a coverage gap on new behavior-bearing surface.

[BUG] The dataclass default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class-definition (module import) time, so every AssignmentSource constructed via `from_integration` gets the worker-process start time instead of the actual queue time. The `queued` field is always stale by however long the process has been running — on a long-lived celery worker it can be hours/days off — and any future staleness-based logic (e.g. dropping stale assignment syncs) silently uses wrong data; it also masks that the value is fixed at import, making it impossible to reason about when an assignment actually originated.

[BUG] `assignment_source.to_dict()` puts a raw `datetime` into celery task kwargs, which the default JSON task serializer cannot encode, so `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async` fails to enqueue when an assignment_source is present. Every inbound integration assignment (the sync_group_assignee_inbound path) enqueues the task with a non-JSON-serializable datetime; on brokers/configurations using the standard JSON serializer the publish raises, and the outbound assignee sync to *other* linked integrations never fires — the core 'allow other integrations to propagate changes outward' requirement is dropped exactly on the path it was built for.

[BUG] `from_dict` performs no type validation, so a payload with `queued` as a string (the result of any serialization round-trip) is accepted and produces an AssignmentSource whose `queued` attribute is a `str`, not a `datetime`. After a worker deserializes kwargs, `parsed_assignment_source.queued` is a string and any datetime arithmetic on it raises TypeError; the `except (ValueError, TypeError)` guard only catches constructor arity problems, never type mismatches, so corrupt sources silently flow into `should_sync` rather than being dropped to None.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds a test only for the same-integration blocking case; there is no test that an assignment sourced from a *different* integration still propagates outbound, which is the explicitly stated primary requirement ('This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward'). A regression that over-blocks (e.g. comparing against the wrong integration_id, or a truthiness bug that blocks all sourced assignments) passes the entire new test suite; the test gap is precisely the acceptance criterion the PR exists to satisfy, and it is unverified.

[ADVISORY] `sync_status_outbound` gains an `assignment_source` parameter but no caller in the diff passes it, and `should_sync("sync_status_outbound")` is never called with a sync_source — status sync cycles remain completely unguarded. The stated goal 'prevent sync-cycles from occurring' is only half-implemented: a status change flowing inbound still triggers outbound status sync back to the originating integration, reintroducing the same loop the PR claims to fix via the assignee path; reviewers/operators will assume cycle protection is in place when it is not.

[ADVISORY] The from_dict test constructs input without the `queued` key and never exercises a `to_dict` → `from_dict` round-trip, which is the only way the field is actually used (it crosses the celery boundary as a dict). The serialization bugs above (datetime encoding failure, string `queued` accepted) are exactly what the round-trip test would have caught; the added test file verifies the dataclass's happy path while leaving the behavior the diff actually depends on untested.

[BUG] The `queued` field default `timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class-definition (module import) time, not per-instance. Every AssignmentSource created after worker startup carries the process boot timestamp as `queued`; consumers of `to_dict()`/analytics get a wrong, shared 'queued at' time — the field never reflects when the assignment actually happened.

[BUG] `assignment_source.to_dict()` embeds a raw `datetime` in Celery task kwargs, which the default JSON task serializer cannot encode. Under a JSON-serialized Celery transport, `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async` raises EncodeError (or the worker fails to decode), so every integration-sourced assignment produces a failed task instead of a sync; with pickle it works only by accident, and if it round-trips as a string, `from_dict` silently accepts a string in a `datetime` field.

[ADVISORY] The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains an `assignment_source` parameter, but no caller in this diff ever passes it and `should_sync` cycle-guarding is only wired into the assignee outbound path. The parameter is dead weight on an abstract method every subclass must now accept, and status-sync inbound→outbound cycles remain unguarded; the next contributor wiring status sync must re-derive the plumbing, and out-of-tree subclass implementations silently drop the argument into `**kwargs`.

[ADVISORY] The cycle-prevention guard in `should_sync` only fires for the `outbound_assignee` attribute path; `sync_group_assignee_inbound`'s status counterpart (`sync_status_inbound`) and the assignee-inbound path that triggers outbound propagation are not plumbed with a source. The stated invariant — preventing sync cycles — is enforced only for assignee outbound; a status change arriving inbound still triggers outbound status sync back to the same integration, reproducing the exact loop this PR claims to fix for the status attribute.

[ADVISORY] `from_dict` returns None on any malformed payload, and the caller in sync_assignee_outbound then treats the assignment as having no source, re-enabling the sync cycle silently. A corrupt or partially-serialized queued payload (e.g., from a pre-deploy producer missing `integration_id`, which `cls(**input_dict)` accepts with a TypeError → None) causes the cycle guard to be silently bypassed instead of logging or failing, so a regression here manifests as the original infinite-sync bug with no signal.

[BUG] The `queued` default `timezone.now()` is evaluated exactly once at class-definition (import) time, so every AssignmentSource instance shares a single stale timestamp instead of recording when the assignment was queued. Every AssignmentSource created after worker boot carries the process-import time as `queued`; any consumer of this timestamp (latency metrics, debugging sync lag) reads a value that is wrong by up to the process lifetime, and the field silently drifts further from reality the longer the process runs — a phantom-derived value with no correct maintainer.

[BUG] `sync_group_assignee_outbound` puts `assignment_source.to_dict()` — a dict containing a raw `datetime` (`queued`) — into Celery task kwargs, which the default JSON task serializer cannot encode. For any user-initiated (or integration-sourced) assignment on a linked group, `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async` fails at serialization/deserialization with 'Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable', so the outbound assignee sync never executes and the external issue's assignee silently diverges from Sentry's — the core feature this PR implements is dead on its main path in JSON-serializer deployments.

[ADVISORY] Cycle prevention (the AssignmentSource guard) is wired only through the assignee path, while `sync_status_outbound` gained an `assignment_source` parameter that no caller in this diff passes, and the inbound status sync path never constructs an AssignmentSource. Status ping-pong between Sentry and a linked tracker (resolve in Jira → inbound resolve in Sentry → outbound resolve pushed back to Jira, and mutatis mutandis) remains possible even though the PR's stated purpose is cross-system sync-cycle prevention; the widened `sync_status_outbound` signature is a ships-inert parameter — every existing and future caller passes nothing, so the guard can never fire for status.

[ADVISORY] `from_dict` performs no type validation, so a payload where `queued` arrives as an ISO string (the shape any JSON round-trip produces) is accepted as a valid AssignmentSource with a string in a datetime-typed field. Once the datetime-serialization issue is 'fixed' by stringifying `queued` at the enqueue boundary, `from_dict` silently reconstructs instances whose `queued` field holds a string, so any code that later treats it as a datetime (comparisons, arithmetic) breaks far from the boundary that caused it; the None-return contract is currently untestable for type drift because nothing is checked.

[BUG] The task calls installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...) but the abstract sync_assignee_outbound in the mixin and all concrete provider implementations were never given an assignment_source parameter — the parameter was instead added to sync_status_outbound. For every real integration (Jira, VSTS, GitHub, etc.), a synced assignee change raises TypeError: sync_assignee_outbound() got an unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source', killing the celery task and breaking assignee sync entirely; only the mock-based tests pass, masking the breakage.

[BUG] The dataclass default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at module import time, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit queued value gets the process-start timestamp, not the time the assignment was made. Any consumer using `queued` to measure sync latency or detect stale re-queued assignments gets garbage values (constant since the worker booted); the field's apparent purpose — recording when the source assignment was queued — is silently unfulfilled.

[BUG] assignment_source.to_dict() embeds a raw datetime (`queued`) in celery task kwargs, a payload crossing the process/queue boundary that JSON-based brokers cannot serialize. With a JSON-serializing broker (or any persisting/inspecting layer), apply_async raises a EncodeError at fan-out time; with redis-pickle brokers it silently works in dev, so the breakage only surfaces in the deployment whose broker differs from the test environment.

[ADVISORY] The abstract sync_status_outbound gained an assignment_source parameter that no caller in the diff passes and no implementation consumes — the parameter appears to have been intended for sync_assignee_outbound (which the task actually calls with it) and drifted onto the wrong method during review iteration. The cycle-prevention intent of the PR is wired to the wrong abstract signature: status-sync has no cycle protection and assignee-sync is broken (see sync_assignee_outbound TypeError), so the stated objective — preventing sync cycles in cross-system synchronization — is not actually achieved by the merged shape of the diff.

[ADVISORY] The updated test asserts sync_assignee_outbound is called with assignment_source=None, which only passes because the integration is mocked; the diff contains no test exercising a real (unmocked) installation end-to-end through the new kwarg. The TypeError that all real implementations hit on the new assignment_source kwarg passes the entire test suite, shipping the breakage to production; the next engineer wiring a real provider integration gets bitten at runtime instead of at CI.

[ADVISORY] sync_group_assignee_outbound serializes AssignmentSource.to_dict() — which contains a raw datetime in the `queued` field — into celery apply_async kwargs, but the worker side reconstructs it via AssignmentSource.from_dict(cls(**input_dict)) which accepts the datetime field as whatever type survives transport. When the JSON serializer is used, the datetime is serialized to an ISO string and the reconstructed AssignmentSource.queued is a str, not a datetime; any consumer of `queued` (e.g. future staleness/cycle-window logic this field exists to support) silently misbehaves, and under strict json the task fails to enqueue entirely — assignment outbound sync silently stops for that issue.

[ADVISORY] AssignmentSource.from_dict performs no type validation of the values it accepts — cls(**input_dict) happily constructs an instance with integration_id as a string, float, or None, and only rejects missing/extra keys. The cycle-prevention check `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id` in should_sync (mixins/issues.py) compares values of potentially mismatched types after a queue round-trip; a deserialized string integration_id makes the equality check always False, so the sync-loop guard the whole feature exists for silently fails and infinite assign/unassign loops between two integrations recur.

[BUG] The `queued` field default `timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class-definition (import) time, so every AssignmentSource instance forever carries the server-process start timestamp instead of the queueing time. All assignment-source metadata records a stale import-time timestamp; the new test_to_dict only asserts `result.get("queued") is not None`, which passes against both correct and broken behavior, so the suite cannot catch this.

[BUG] `assignment_source.to_dict()` puts a raw `datetime` (from `asdict` on the `queued` field) into Celery `apply_async` kwargs, which the default JSON task serializer cannot encode, so the outbound-assignee task fails to enqueue whenever an assignment_source is set. Every cross-integration assignee sync triggered via a source-carrying assignment (the feature this diff adds) raises a serialization error at enqueue time in JSON-serialized deployments; no test in the diff exercises the task path with a non-None assignment_source, so this is never hit.

[ADVISORY] The new cycle-prevention branch in `should_sync` (issues.py) is tested only for the matching-integration rejection path; no test in the diff triggers the positive propagation path with a non-None, non-matching `AssignmentSource` (different integration_id), which is the behavior the new code comment explicitly promises to preserve. A regression that over-blocks sync (e.g. comparing on source_name, or inverting the inequality so all sourced assignments are dropped for other integrations too) passes the full suite; the 'still allow other integrations to propagate outward' claim is entirely unverified.

[ADVISORY] The `deassign` path's new `assignment_source` parameter threading is never tested with a non-None source; the only deassign test asserts `assignment_source=None` (test_assignee_sync_outbound_unassign, line ~271-274), and the new matching-source test covers only `assign`, not `deassign`. The inbound-unassign loop in sync.py (lines ~96-99) that stamps `AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` on deassign is the main producer of sourced deassignments, and no test verifies that a subsequent deassign from the same integration is suppressed — the unassign half of the sync-cycle fix is unverified.

[ADVISORY] The AssignmentSource test suite never tests the to_dict → from_dict round-trip, and test_to_dict's `assert result.get("queued") is not None` is a bare existence check that passes regardless of the queued value's correctness or serializability. The exact serialization contract the Celery task path depends on (assignment_source_dict carrying a datetime) is the one path with zero coverage — the task-level deserialization in sync_assignee_outbound.py lines ~53-56 is also untested, so any drift between what to_dict emits and what from_dict accepts (or what the broker can serialize) fails silently in production.

[BUG] AssignmentSource.to_dict() emits a raw datetime under the `queued` key, which cannot be serialized by Celery's JSON task transport, so apply_async fails at enqueue time. In sync_group_assignee_outbound (src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:137-143), assignment_source.to_dict() is placed directly into task kwargs; when the default JSON serializer is used, serializing the datetime raises EncodeError and the outbound assignee sync task is never enqueued, silently breaking assignee sync (or, on brokers that do ship it, from_dict re-materializes `queued` as a string that the `datetime`-typed field silently accepts, losing type fidelity).

[BUG] The task signature gains a new `assignment_source_dict` kwarg that old workers do not accept, breaking rolling deploys. During a rolling deploy, a new-code producer calls sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async with kwargs including assignment_source_dict while old-code workers are still draining the queue; the old worker's function does not have the parameter, the task raises TypeError, and assignee-sync tasks fail (and retry-loop if a retry policy is set) until every worker is upgraded — an expand-phase violation with no compatibility window.

[BUG] sync_group_assignee_outbound passes assignment_source.to_dict() containing a raw datetime (`queued`) as an apply_async kwarg, which the celery JSON serializer cannot encode, so the sync task fails at publish time and the assignee sync is silently dropped while the caller (GroupAssignee.objects.assign) reports success. When the JSON task serializer is in use (Sentry's hardening direction), every assign/deassign with an inbound assignment_source raises a serialization error inside the fire-and-forget apply_async; the group is still assigned locally, but the outbound sync to OTHER linked integrations never runs and no error reaches the user — the exact partial-success the cycle-prevention design is meant to preserve. The fix is to omit `queued` from to_dict (or serialize it to an ISO string), since nothing consumes it.

[BUG] The `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` dataclass default is evaluated exactly once at module import, so every AssignmentSource instance created in a long-lived worker process carries the process-start timestamp instead of the actual queue time. Any future consumer of `queued` (its stated purpose is queue-time tracking) computes staleness against the worker boot time rather than enqueue time; on a multi-day-lived process, deltas are wrong by hours-to-days with no error surfaced. Currently nothing reads `queued`, so impact is latent, but the field's value is already silently wrong at every construction site.

[ADVISORY] from_dict does not convert a `queued` value back to a datetime, so a dict that has round-tripped through JSON (if the serialization failure above is fixed by isoformat-string) reconstructs AssignmentSource with queued as a str, and from_dict also swallows all TypeError/ValueError without logging, so malformed payloads (including a string-typed `queued`) parse 'successfully' as a source whose types violate the dataclass contract. A consumer that later does arithmetic or comparisons on `queued` (e.g. staleness-based dedup) gets a TypeError crash in a task, or the silent None return masks a payload bug with no log line to diagnose why cycle-prevention stopped working.

[ADVISORY] The inbound assignment path passes AssignmentSource into GroupAssignee.objects.assign/deassign, which fans out to sync_group_assignee_outbound for every linked external issue — but the assignment_source threading is only used for cycle-suppression on the assignee dimension; if from_dict returns None on a corrupt payload, should_sync's cycle check is silently skipped and a sync cycle between two integrations can re-emerge with no telemetry that parsing failed. Operators debugging an assignee ping-pong loop between integrations get no signal that a malformed assignment_source_dict silently disabled the guard; the fallback (None → sync proceeds) is the fail-open direction for a cycle-prevention mechanism.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py`, the dataclass defines `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` (line shown in diff). In Python dataclasses, this default expression is evaluated once at class definition/import time, not per instance creation. Since `AssignmentSource.from_integration()` does not pass `queued`, every instance created that way will reuse the same timestamp (worker start/import time) rather than the actual creation time. This is a real correctness defect; it should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` to get a fresh timestamp per instance.

With a JSON-based task serializer, a raw `datetime` is not JSON-serializable and would fail to enqueue when `assignment_source` is provided (notably on the inbound integration path where `AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` is always set).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] sync_group_assignee_outbound passes assignment_source.to_dict() containing a raw datetime (`queued`) as an apply_async kwarg, which the celery JSON serializer cannot encode, so the sync task fails at publish time and the assignee sync is silently dropped while the caller (GroupAssignee.objects.assign) reports success. When the JSON task serializer is in use (Sentry's hardening direction), every assign/deassign with an inbound assignment_source raises a serialization error inside the fire-and-forget apply_async; the group is still assigned locally, but the outbound sync to OTHER linked integrations never runs and no error reaches the user — the exact partial-success the cycle-prevention design is meant to preserve. The fix is to omit `queued` from to_dict (or serialize it to an ISO string), since nothing consumes it.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, which includes `queued` as a `datetime` (`queued: datetime = timezone.now()`). `sync_group_assignee_outbound()` then passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` directly into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)` as `assignment_source_dict`. If the Celery task serializer is JSON (a common/hardened configuration), a raw Python `datetime` is not JSON-serializable, so publishing the task would fail at enqueue time. Nothing in the diff converts `queued` to a string or omits it, and the new tests even assert `queued` is present, reinforcing that the payload contains a datetime.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` dataclass default is evaluated exactly once at module import, so every AssignmentSource instance created in a long-lived worker process carries the process-start timestamp instead of the actual queue time. Any future consumer of `queued` (its stated purpose is queue-time tracking) computes staleness against the worker boot time rather than enqueue time; on a multi-day-lived process, deltas are wrong by hours-to-days with no error surfaced. Currently nothing reads `queued`, so impact is latent, but the field's value is already silently wrong at every construction site.

adjudication.rationale: In `AssignmentSource` (new file `src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py`), the dataclass field is declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. This calls `timezone.now()` at class definition/import time, so all instances created in a long-lived process will share the same `queued` timestamp rather than the creation/enqueue time. Dataclasses require `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` to get a per-instance timestamp, making the finding a real correctness defect introduced by the diff.

A consumer that later does arithmetic or comparisons on `queued` (e.g. staleness-based dedup) gets a TypeError crash in a task, or the silent None return masks a payload bug with no log line to diagnose why cycle-prevention stopped working.

Because dataclass type hints aren’t enforced at runtime, a payload with `queued` as a string (e.g., after JSON round-tripping) would be accepted and produce an `AssignmentSource` whose `queued` is not a `datetime`, and there’s no validation/logging to surface malformed payloads. However, in this diff `queued` is not actually used anywhere (cycle-prevention only checks `integration_id` in `should_sync`), so the finding’s claimed downstream crashes/dedup behavior aren’t verifiable from the shown changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The inbound assignment path passes AssignmentSource into GroupAssignee.objects.assign/deassign, which fans out to sync_group_assignee_outbound for every linked external issue — but the assignment_source threading is only used for cycle-suppression on the assignee dimension; if from_dict returns None on a corrupt payload, should_sync's cycle check is silently skipped and a sync cycle between two integrations can re-emerge with no telemetry that parsing failed. Operators debugging an assignee ping-pong loop between integrations get no signal that a malformed assignment_source_dict silently disabled the guard; the fallback (None → sync proceeds) is the fail-open direction for a cycle-prevention mechanism.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `sync_assignee_outbound` reconstructs the source via `AssignmentSource.from_dict(...)` and, on parse failure, sets `parsed_assignment_source=None` (returns `None` on `ValueError`/`TypeError`) with no logging. `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync(..., sync_source)` only suppresses cycles when `sync_source` is present and matches `self.org_integration.integration_id`; if parsing yields `None`, that guard is skipped and outbound sync can proceed. This is a real, diff-grounded edge-case/operability concern (fail-open + no telemetry), but it only manifests with malformed payloads and is not a directly verifiable correctness break in normal flows shown in the diff.
